title: Outsourced Accounts Receivable: Who Invoices and Who Collects
summary: Outsourced accounts receivable services cover invoicing, payment reminders, and cash application. See what a provider should own and where your team stays.
body_markdown:
## What Outsourced Accounts Receivable Covers


Outsourced accounts receivable services move the repeatable order-to-cash work to an external accounting team while the receivable and the customer stay yours. Accounts receivable outsourcing covers the operations, not the ownership. The provider runs the sequence. You keep the credit policy, the customer relationship, and every dollar sitting on your balance sheet.


Most buyers searching for outsourced invoicing and collections expect two different jobs from one vendor, so it helps to see the scope written out.


- **Invoice creation and delivery.** Built off the signed contract, the billing platform, or the usage file, and sent in your templates.
- **Payment tracking and reminder sequences.** Sent in your name, on a cadence you approved in advance.
- **Cash application and reconciliation.** Daily matching of receipts to open invoices, with an exception queue for what does not match.
- **Dispute intake and reason coding.** Logged and routed, never decided by the provider.
- **Credit memo processing.** Issued by the provider against a dollar authority limit you set.
- **AR aging and allowance support.** Weekly or monthly aging, plus the schedule your close needs.


Three adjacent services get sold under similar names. None of them are this.


- **Not receivables financing.** Factoring sells the invoice at a discount and AR lending borrows against the balance. Both are capital decisions for the CFO or the board, not an operations decision about who sends the reminder.
- **Not a collections agency.** An agency works defaulted paper on contingency. That is a late-stage exception, not the plan.
- **Not an AP versus AR explainer.** If this is the search you ran, you already know what a receivable is. You’re deciding who runs it.


The practical floor sits around 100 to 150 invoices a month. Below that, oversight overhead tends to cancel the saving. The usual triggers to act are days sales outstanding drifting past 45 to 50 days, or a founder personally chasing payments between board meetings.


Late payment is the background condition, not the exception. Atradius found in its[2026 research on US B2B payment practices](https://group.atradius.com/knowledge-and-research/reports/b2b-payment-practices-trends-in-the-us-2026) that late payments affect an average of 22% of US B2B receivables, that about seven in ten companies still face them, and that 55% of suppliers attribute the delay to customer liquidity rather than a broken process. A fifth of your ledger is late by default. Someone has to work it every week.


That is the argument for putting receivables inside the engagement that already closes your books rather than beside it. It’s one layer of[the full finance function delivered as a single engagement](https://www.indinero.com/blog/what-is-finance-as-a-service/) , which is how indinero scopes it.


## The Order-to-Cash Steps a Provider Can Own


Order to cash is a sequence, and a provider can own it from invoice through aging without ever owning a customer. Walk the steps in order, and name the handoff in each one.


- **Invoice generation.** The provider builds the invoice off the signed contract, the billing system, or the usage file. For subscription businesses, billing terms and revenue recognition diverge right here, so ask who maintains the billing schedule when a contract is amended mid-term.
- **Invoice delivery.** Still a measurable variable. The 2026 Billtrust accounts receivable benchmark, drawn from roughly $1 trillion in annual B2B transactions, puts electronic invoice delivery at 81.76% in 2025, up from 79.65% the year before. The remaining fifth is where delivery failures and “we never got it” disputes live.
- **Payment reminder sequences.** A pre-due reminder, a due-date notice, then a defined cadence after. The sequence should be documented and approved by you, never improvised account by account.
- **Cash application and unapplied cash.** The least visible step and the one that quietly breaks the close. The same benchmark reports 2025 envelope match at 88.48% and line-item match at 93.76%. The gap is the exception queue, and every unmatched payment is cash that ties out at the bank and not at the customer level.
- **Dispute logging.** The provider codes the reason and routes it. A recurring short-pay reason is usually a contract or delivery problem, not a collections problem.
- **Credit memos.** Issued by the provider, approved by you, against a threshold set in writing before go-live.
- **Aging and the allowance.** Under ASC 326, private companies carry an allowance for expected credit losses on ordinary trade receivables from the day the receivable is recognized, and a loss-rate approach built on aging buckets is an accepted method. PwC’s guidance on[applying CECL to trade receivables](https://viewpoint.pwc.com/dt/us/en/pwc/accounting_guides/loans_and_investment/loans_and_investment_US/chapter_7_current_ex_US/7_7-Application-of-CECL-to-trade-receivables.html) walks the provision-matrix mechanics.


That last step is the whole case for keeping AR inside the accounting engagement instead of bolting on a separate AR vendor. The same team that ages the ledger builds the allowance and books the entry.


Days sales outstanding is the scoreboard here, not the subject. The Billtrust benchmark puts average client DSO at 39 days in 2025, down from 45, against an industry median of 46 and top performers at 28. Track it alongside[the accounts receivable turnover ratio](https://www.indinero.com/blog/accounts-receivable-turnover-ratio/) , then take the strategy conversation over to[working capital and the cash conversion cycle](https://www.indinero.com/blog/working-capital-optimization/) , which is where the levers actually sit.


## Where a Provider’s Payment Reminders Should Stop


A provider can send a reminder and reconcile the cash. It should not be the voice that decides whether an account renews. That line is the honest center of the engagement, and it belongs in the scope document rather than in a bad quarter’s post-mortem.


This isn’t just a question of who sends the invoice. It’s a question of who owns the conversation when the invoice goes unpaid.


A workable escalation ladder, written as policy:


- **Days 1 to 30.** The provider owns it. Templated reminders in your name and tone, delivery confirmation, dispute intake.
- **Days 31 to 60.** The provider still runs outreach, but every contact is visible to your account owner. Any disputed or at-risk account exits the sequence and goes to a named person on your side.
- **Day 61 and beyond.** Your account manager or founder owns the conversation. The provider supports with documentation, payment plan tracking, and the aging.
- **Agency referral.** The exception, agreed in writing, with a dollar floor and a named approver.


Four controls make that boundary real rather than aspirational. Approved templates and tone. A named escalation owner on each side. A strategic-account exclusion list that never enters the automated sequence. Visibility into every message sent on your behalf.


One legal distinction removes a common fear. The Fair Debt Collection Practices Act applies to obligations incurred primarily for personal, family, or household purposes under[15 U.S.C. 1692a(5)](https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/15/1692a) . Commercial B2B debt sits outside that definition, and the statute also excludes from “debt collector” a person collecting a debt that was not in default when they took it on. That is exactly the posture of an accounting provider invoicing on your behalf. State law and contract terms still govern conduct, so this is not a license to be aggressive.


It is also why a third-party agency is the exception and not the recommendation. Commercial collection agencies work on contingency, commonly 20% to 35% of recovery on B2B accounts and up to 50% on aged or small balances. Routing a 45-day invoice there surrenders a fifth to a third of the balance and converts a customer into a defendant. The first 60 days belong inside the engagement.


Data access is the other boundary worth writing down. A provider working your AR touches customer contact data, contract terms, and bank remittance detail, so ask for a SOC 2 report scoped to security and confidentiality at minimum. Ask who sits above the sequence reviewing the aging, too. That oversight layer is what[outsourced controller services](https://www.indinero.com/blog/outsourced-controller-services/) are built to supply.


## AR Outsourcing vs AR Automation Software


AR outsourcing vs AR automation is a scope and volume question, not a tool war. Software executes rules. A team handles the exceptions that rules can’t close.


Dimension AR automation software An outsourced AR team


Core job Runs the reminder sequence, matches payments to invoices, surfaces the aging Works the exceptions, chases disputes, resolves unapplied cash, prepares allowance support


Published cost Roughly $500 to $5,000 a month for small to mid-size businesses, quote-only at mid-market and above Per invoice, monthly retainer, dedicated FTE, or hourly


Strongest when Volume is high, terms are standard, the data is clean Contracts are messy and one person does AR between close tasks


Weakest when Exceptions outnumber rules Volume is low enough that oversight costs more than it saves


What it will not do Close your books Replace your customer relationship


Pick by what you actually have on hand:


- **High volume, standard terms, clean data, a controller with time.** Automate first. The rules will close most of it.
- **Moderate volume, messy contracts, AR squeezed between close tasks.** Outsource first. Software won’t fix a missing process.
- **Growing volume and a close that’s already late.** Both, in that order. Automation for the sequence, a team for the exception queue.
- **Under roughly 100 invoices a month.** Neither yet. Tighten terms and invoice on time.


The honest case for running both is the exception rate. Even at a 93.76% line-item match rate, the residual is manual investigation, and that residual is where unapplied cash accumulates and the aging stops being trustworthy. Software lowers the exception count. It does not work the queue.


There’s a structural point underneath the comparison. An AR-only vendor and an AR automation platform both stop at the ledger, and neither one closes your books. When receivables sit in the same engagement as[bookkeeping and the monthly close](https://www.indinero.com/services/online-bookkeeping-services/) , the aging, the allowance, and the revenue reconciliation are produced by one team working one set of records.


## What Outsourced AR Costs and How It Is Priced


Published 2026 pricing for outsourced AR clusters into four models, and the model you’re quoted tells you more than the number does.


Pricing model Published band Best fit


Per invoice $0.50 to $3.50 per invoice at the standard end, $2 to $8 at the higher-touch end High volume, standardized billing


Monthly retainer $2,500 to $15,000 and up per month Stable receivables, a defined task list


Dedicated FTE $1,500 to $5,000 per month per person Complex workflows needing a named owner


Hourly $8 to $30 per hour Project work, variable volume


Blended annual cost for a small to mid-size business lands around $12,000 to $30,000 for full AR scope, scaling from there with invoice volume and customer count.


Contingency pricing is the one to flag. Percentage of recovery is standard for collections agencies at 20% to 50% depending on age and balance, and it’s unusual inside an accounting engagement. The reason is incentive alignment. A contingency fee pays for recovery on aged paper. It doesn’t pay for an invoice that goes out correctly on day one, a payment applied the day it lands, or an allowance that ties to the aging. Those are the things that keep receivables from aging at all, and they get priced as scope, not as commission.


Then there’s the in-house anchor. Billing and posting clerks (SOC 43-3021) are the closest occupation to an AR or billing clerk, and the[Bureau of Labor Statistics occupational wage estimates](https://www.bls.gov/oes/2023/may/oes433021.htm) put national employment at 430,220, the mean annual wage at $47,120, and the median at $45,590, with the 75th percentile at $52,170. More recent federal wage data moves the median to roughly $48,500.


Salary isn’t the cost. Add employer payroll taxes, benefits, software seats, PTO coverage, and the hours your controller spends supervising and rehiring, and one AR seat sits meaningfully above the wage line. Research across US midsize businesses has put roughly two-thirds of them at an average of 14 hours a week on administrative work tied to collecting payments, which is time that shows up on somebody’s salary line whether you book it there or not. Run the retainer against a fully loaded seat, minus the coverage risk of a single point of failure who takes vacation during close week. If that supervision burden is the real cost,[outsourced controller services](https://www.indinero.com/blog/outsourced-controller-services/) are the layer to price alongside it.


## How Indinero Runs Receivables Inside the Engagement


Indinero runs receivables as one layer of a bundled finance function, so the aging you chase and the ledger you close are the same record. Bookkeeping, GAAP close, business tax, and CFO-level advisory sit in one engagement with one CPA-led team. There’s no vendor seam between the person who applies the cash and the person who books the allowance.


That matters most at the two places AR usually breaks. Unapplied cash gets resolved by people who also own the trial balance, so a payment doesn’t sit in suspense until someone notices during close. The aging that feeds your ASC 326 allowance is built by the team that signs off on the financials, not handed across a contract boundary and re-keyed.


The rhythm is a year-round extension of your finance team rather than a transactional vendor relationship. Five things get settled before the first invoice goes out.


1. **System of record.** Who invoices from which system, who maintains the billing schedule, and what happens on a mid-term contract amendment.
2. **Templates and tone.** Your templates, your voice, approved in advance.
3. **The sequence and the exclusion list.** Exact cadence and channel for days 1 to 30 and 31 to 60, with strategic accounts named and kept out of it.
4. **The escalation trigger.** Day count, dollar threshold, and dispute flag that move an account to your owner, with a named person on each side.
5. **Close deliverables.** Aging by a stated business day, unapplied cash cleared inside a stated window, allowance support reconciled to the same buckets.


Track DSO as the headline, but the operational tells are unapplied cash as a percentage of receipts, first-pass match rate, dispute aging by reason code, and how many accounts reach day 61 without an escalation being raised.


The track record behind that: continuous operations since 2009, SOC 2 compliant (2026), and a 5-star Clutch rating. Pricing starts at $750/mo, and receivables scope is quoted against your invoice volume and billing complexity rather than as a percentage of what gets collected. You can see how the layer underneath it is scoped on the[online bookkeeping services](https://www.indinero.com/services/online-bookkeeping-services/) page.


Receivables shouldn’t be something you find out about on a renewal call. If your aging and your ledger have stopped agreeing, that’s worth a conversation.


## Frequently asked questions


Controllers evaluating outsourced accounts receivable services tend to arrive with the same handful of questions, and most of them are about the boundary rather than the scope. These are the ones that come up most often in scoping calls. Each answer reflects how we’d handle it inside an engagement, not a generic industry position.


### Is outsourced accounts receivable the same as hiring a collections agency?


No, outsourced accounts receivable is ongoing invoicing and cash application work, while a collections agency works defaulted accounts on contingency. Agency fees commonly run 20% to 35% of recovery on B2B accounts, and up to 50% on aged or small balances. Indinero treats an agency referral as a written exception with a dollar floor and a named approver, because the first 60 days of an aging belong inside the engagement that closes your books.


### Will our customers know that invoicing is handled outside the company?


Usually not, because invoices and payment reminders go out in your templates, your name, and your tone on a cadence you approve in advance. The customer relationship stays yours. Strategic accounts can be named on an exclusion list that never enters the automated sequence, and you keep visibility into every message sent on your behalf. Indinero settles templates, tone, and the exclusion list before the first invoice goes out.


### How much does outsourced accounts receivable cost each month?


Outsourced accounts receivable is priced per invoice at roughly $0.50 to $8, or on a monthly retainer of about $2,500 to $15,000. Blended annual cost for a small to mid-size business lands around $12,000 to $30,000 for full scope. Indinero pricing starts at $750/mo, and receivables scope is quoted against your invoice volume and billing complexity rather than as a percentage of what gets collected.


### Can we outsource receivables without changing our billing system?


Yes, most outsourced AR engagements run inside your existing billing system, so the provider works in your tools instead of migrating you onto theirs. Settle the system of record first. Name who invoices from which system, who maintains the billing schedule, and what happens when a contract is amended mid-term. Indinero works inside the ledger you already use, whether that’s QuickBooks, Xero, or NetSuite, so receivables sit on the same records that feed your close.


### Who decides when an unpaid invoice goes to a collections agency?


You decide, never the provider, under a written escalation policy that sets a dollar floor, an account age, and a named approver. A workable ladder gives the provider days 1 to 30, keeps days 31 to 60 visible to your account owner, and moves day 61 to your side. Indinero puts that trigger in the scope document before go-live, because agency referral is the exception, not the plan.


### Does outsourced AR work for usage-based or milestone billing?


Yes, outsourced AR handles usage-based and milestone billing, as long as the invoice source and the billing schedule owner are defined up front. These models generate more exceptions, which is exactly where a team beats a rules engine. Usage files, mid-term amendments, and milestone acceptance disputes don’t close themselves. Because indinero also books revenue and closes the month, billing terms and revenue recognition get reconciled by one team.


### How soon should days sales outstanding improve after the handover?


Expect days sales outstanding to move after two to three full billing cycles, roughly 60 to 90 days from handover. Receivables already in the aging carry their old terms, so indinero’s first cycle mostly fixes delivery and cash application, with unapplied cash and first-pass match rate as the earlier tells. For reference, the 2026 Billtrust benchmark puts average DSO at 39 days in 2025 against an industry median of 46 and top performers at 28.
